summary: Lays out a conceptual framework and rules of thumb for working groups dealing with intellectual property rights issues. It records examples of how the IETF has handled such issues in the past. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a team gets stuck on who owns an idea, this is a handbook of tips and examples from earlier teams, so they know sensible ways to handle it.

questions: how should working groups handle ipr
what is a third party ipr disclosure
does the ietf judge patent validity
subtitle: Case studies and rules of thumb to help IETF working groups decide what to do about patents and other IPR claims.

tldr.problem: Most useful technology brought to the IETF now carries some intellectual property claim, yet working groups have almost no formal rules for handling such claims.
tldr.mechanism: The memo offers six case studies from past working groups and draws general principles from them: think about IPR early, weigh licensing terms above claim validity, and ask claimants to be explicit.
tldr.outcome: It sets no rules. It gives working groups information to make their own informed decisions, and it updates RFC 2026.

today: RFC 3669 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 2026. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It points to RFC 3667 and RFC 3668 for the actual author and claimant procedures.

sections.title: Introduction and Goal
sections.content:
RFC 3669 lays out a conceptual framework and rules of thumb for IETF working groups dealing with Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) issues. The aim is a balance between the needs of IPR claimants and the implementers of IETF standards. It calls itself a record of the "running code" of the IETF process.

It does not cover procedures for document authors or claimants; those are in two other memos, on submission rights (RFC 3667) and IPR in the IETF (RFC 3668). This one is for working groups deciding what to do about technology contributions that come with IPR claims. It does not try to make rules, only to give groups information and then step out of the way.
sections.plainLanguage: This guide is not a rulebook. It is a collection of tips so a group can decide for itself what to do when someone says they own an idea.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The IETF has traditionally tried to avoid technology protected by IPR claims, but the Internet has run on IPR-impacted technology from the start. The memo says that nowadays the majority of useful technologies brought to the IETF have some IPR claim. Choosing an unaffected alternative can sometimes produce a weaker Internet, and it is not always wrong to pick IPR-impacted technology if the choice is made knowingly.

The IETF is not a membership organization, so it cannot require members to sign agreements or insist on royalty-free licensing. It can meet four situations at almost any time: a submitter notes their own claim, another participant claims the document is covered by their IPR, a participant notes a claim by an unaffiliated party, or an outsider who has been monitoring comes forward.

Working groups have essentially one rule to invoke: individuals may not take part in activities on a technology if they do not disclose known IPR. Beyond that they can only make recommendations and requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost every good idea brought to the group already has an owner who might want to be paid. The group cannot force anyone to sign a promise, so it has to be careful and smart.

sections.title: Case Studies
sections.content:
Six working group experiences are described, each with lessons.

  • PPP CCP and ECP: the group adopted patented technology, and a variance procedure was used to get an exception to the old requirement for specific licensing assurances. Lesson: claimants may resist public statements of terms, and forced statements tend to be worst-case.
  • IPS (IP Storage): after choosing SRP, more possible claims surfaced and licensing terms stayed vague, so the group decided not to use SRP after all. Lesson: claims can appear at any time, so seek clarification.
  • PEM and PKI: public key patents were a known issue, but no alternative came close, and the patents would expire within a few years. Lesson: IPR is one factor among many, and its lifecycle matters.
  • VRRP: the group went ahead despite a claimant's stated position, with no evidence it considered the implications. Lesson: never disregard claims without good cause.
  • SecSH: a trademark holder wanted the IETF to stop using "SSH" in names. The group weighed the risk and kept the names.
  • IDN: the group investigated several claims, talked with the claimant, discussed prior art on its list, and gradually concluded its documents did not infringe. Lesson: pushing claimants to explain their claims and terms can help.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo tells six true stories about earlier groups. Some kept going, one dropped a design, and the lesson is to ask questions, think carefully and not just ignore the problem.

sections.title: General Principles
sections.content:
Every working group must follow its own consensus and take IPR seriously, including the needs of future implementers who are not part of the group. The memo lists times to think about IPR: when examining a technology, adopting a draft, choosing between drafts, depending on outside technology, or comparing kinds of IPR. At those times the group is strongly encouraged to solicit disclosure of IPR claims and licensing terms.

IPR is one input to evaluating a technology. The question is how much it limits usefulness, so the key points are whether the claim is relevant and under what terms the technology can be used. Neither the IETF nor a working group takes a stance on the validity of any claim; individuals form their own opinions, though the group may make choices based on perceived risk.

Perfect knowledge is not a worthwhile goal, because it is impossible to prove a technology is not covered by any claim. The memo says that licensing terms are a more significant consideration than claim validity, and "rough" confidence is usually good enough.

For a patent already granted, the IETF can reasonably expect the patent number and possibly the relevant document sections. For a pending patent it can expect only that it exists, the related documents and perhaps a statement about licensing terms.
sections.plainLanguage: The group does not decide who is right about who owns an idea. It just asks whether using the idea would be too costly or risky, and it cares most about how the owner will let others use it.

sections.title: Licensing Terms
sections.content:
Licensing terms range from no license required to prohibitive. The memo lists a rough order of preference that working groups tend to show, and notes it is not a rule. From best to worst: no license required; licensed with no restrictions; no material restrictions; licensed for a field of use only; royalty-free with reasonable and non-discriminatory terms; reasonable and non-discriminatory terms (possibly with a royalty); otherwise licensable; not licensable; and not available under any conditions.

Many claimants do not like to publish specific terms, so do not expect detailed blanket terms. Vague terms are not necessarily worse in practice. Words such as "reasonable", "fair" and "non-discriminatory" have no objective legal or financial definition, so the best way to learn what a claimant means is to ask explicitly. The memo also mentions reciprocity and defensive suspension as restrictions to consult a legal adviser about.
sections.plainLanguage: Owners can say "free for everybody" or "you must pay" or "no way". Groups like the free kind best, and when an owner says "fair price" it is smart to ask what that really means.

sections.title: Third-Party Disclosure
sections.content:
It is good to tell the IETF about relevant IPR claims even when they are not your own. But third-party disclosure is a potential denial of service threat to a working group, because it can distract the group and slow its work. Groups should evaluate such disclosures with that in mind, and chairs should be willing to discipline those who misuse the system. Anyone who feels unfairly blocked may take the matter to the Area Directors or the IESG.

The advice for someone thinking of disclosing is to write to the working group chairs first, bring the issue to the group and to the claimant if that is not too hard, and only then submit a third-party disclosure if sure the claim applies. Do not raise unrelated claims, and keep each message substantive and focused on one specific issue.

On security, the memo says it concerns IETF process, not any particular technology. A technology's security considerations should be weighed as one part of evaluating it, just as IPR is, but they are not issues of security with the IPR procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: If you notice someone else owns an idea the group is using, you should tell the group leaders politely first. Shouting about it right away could distract everyone from their work.
